claim: Tardigrades are animals that can survive extreme conditions.
source: Tardigrades, also known as water bears, are animals that can survive extreme conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about tardigrades presented in the abstract, drawing from established scientific knowledge about these organisms.

claim: The tardigrade Ramazzottius varieornatus contains a unique nuclear protein termed Dsup.
source: The tardigrade Ramazzottius varieornatus contains a unique nuclear protein termed Dsup, for damage suppressor, which can increase the resistance of human cells to DNA damage under conditions, such as ionizing radiation or hydrogen peroxide treatment, that generate hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hashimoto et al., 2016) and is a foundational statement for the study.

claim: Dsup can increase the resistance of human cells to DNA damage under conditions such as ionizing radiation or hydrogen peroxide treatment that generate hydroxyl radicals.
source: The tardigrade Ramazzottius varieornatus contains a unique nuclear protein termed Dsup, for damage suppressor, which can increase the resistance of human cells to DNA damage under conditions, such as ionizing radiation or hydrogen peroxide treatment, that generate hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This claim is based on prior published work (Hashimoto et al., 2016) as cited in the introduction.

claim: R. varieornatus Dsup is a nucleosome-binding protein.
source: Here we find that R. varieornatus Dsup is a nucleosome-binding protein that protects chromatin from hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from gel mobility shift assays shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: R. varieornatus Dsup protects chromatin from hydroxyl radicals.
source: Here we find that R. varieornatus Dsup is a nucleosome-binding protein that protects chromatin from hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from hydroxyl radical cleavage assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: A Dsup ortholog from the tardigrade Hypsibius exemplaris binds to nucleosomes.
source: Moreover, a Dsup ortholog from the tardigrade Hypsibius exemplaris similarly binds to nucleosomes and protects DNA from hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from gel mobility shift assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A Dsup ortholog from the tardigrade Hypsibius exemplaris protects DNA from hydroxyl radicals.
source: Moreover, a Dsup ortholog from the tardigrade Hypsibius exemplaris similarly binds to nucleosomes and protects DNA from hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from hydroxyl radical cleavage assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A conserved region in Dsup proteins exhibits sequence similarity to the nucleosome-binding domain of vertebrate HMGN proteins.
source: Strikingly, a conserved region in Dsup proteins exhibits sequence similarity to the nucleosome-binding domain of vertebrate HMGN proteins and is functionally important for nucleosome binding and hydroxyl radical protection.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The conserved region in Dsup proteins that is similar to HMGN is functionally important for nucleosome binding.
source: Strikingly, a conserved region in Dsup proteins exhibits sequence similarity to the nucleosome-binding domain of vertebrate HMGN proteins and is functionally important for nucleosome binding and hydroxyl radical protection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with mutant Dsup proteins shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The conserved region in Dsup proteins that is similar to HMGN is functionally important for hydroxyl radical protection.
source: Strikingly, a conserved region in Dsup proteins exhibits sequence similarity to the nucleosome-binding domain of vertebrate HMGN proteins and is functionally important for nucleosome binding and hydroxyl radical protection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with mutant Dsup proteins shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Dsup promotes the survival of tardigrades under diverse conditions by binding to nucleosomes and protecting chromosomal DNA from hydroxyl radicals.
source: These findings suggest that Dsup promotes the survival of tardigrades under diverse conditions by a direct mechanism that involves binding to nucleosomes and protecting chromosomal DNA from hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and inference about the biological role of Dsup.

claim: Tardigrades are small invertebrate animals found in marine, freshwater, and terrestrial habitats throughout the Earth.
source: Tardigrades, which are also known as water bears or moss piglets, are small invertebrate animals that are found in marine, freshwater, and terrestrial habitats throughout the Earth (reviewed in Guidetti et al., 2012; Møbjerg et al., 2011; Weronika and Łukasz, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles about tardigrades.

claim: Tardigrades are typically about 0.1 to 1 mm in length.
source: They are typically about 0.1 to 1 mm in length, and comprise a head segment in addition to four body segments that each contains two legs with claws.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about tardigrade morphology based on established knowledge.

claim: Tardigrades comprise a head segment in addition to four body segments that each contains two legs with claws.
source: They are typically about 0.1 to 1 mm in length, and comprise a head segment in addition to four body segments that each contains two legs with claws.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about tardigrade morphology based on established knowledge.

claim: Terrestrial tardigrades require a thin film of water to remain active.
source: Terrestrial tardigrades require a thin film of water to remain active.
evidence: This is a statement about tardigrade biology based on established knowledge.

claim: In the absence of water, tardigrades undergo anhydrobiosis into a dormant dehydrated state from which they can be rehydrated to an active form.
source: In the absence of water, they undergo anhydrobiosis into a dormant dehydrated state from which they can be rehydrated to an active form.
evidence: This is a statement about tardigrade biology based on established knowledge.

claim: In the anhydrobiotic state, tardigrades are resistant to extreme conditions of heat, cold, vacuum, pressure, radiation, and chemical treatments.
source: In the anhydrobiotic state, tardigrades are resistant to extreme conditions of heat, cold, vacuum, pressure, radiation, and chemical treatments.
evidence: This is a statement about tardigrade biology based on established knowledge.

claim: Tardigrades have been found to survive exposure to the vacuum and radiation of outer space.
source: Remarkably, they have been found to survive exposure to the vacuum and radiation of outer space (Jönsson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The genomes of Ramazzottius varieornatus and Hypsibius exemplaris have been sequenced.
source: The molecular analysis of tardigrades has been advanced by the sequencing of the genomes of Ramazzottius varieornatus (Hashimoto et al., 2016) and Hypsibius exemplaris (Yoshida et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genome sequencing publications.

claim: The strain of tardigrades designated as Hypsibius dujardini in Yoshida et al. (2017) has since been found to be a new species now termed Hypsibius exemplaris.
source: [Note: the strain of tardigrades that was designated as Hypsibius dujardini in Yoshida et al. (2017) has since been found to be a new species that is now termed Hypsibius exemplaris (GĄsiorek et al., 2018). We will use the new terminology in this paper.]
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a taxonomic study.

claim: Dsup is a highly charged and largely unstructured nuclear protein that binds to DNA.
source: Dsup is a highly charged and largely unstructured nuclear protein that binds to DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hashimoto et al., 2016; Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017).

claim: Expression of Dsup gene in human cells was observed to decrease DNA fragmentation induced by X-ray irradiation or treatment with hydrogen peroxide.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of Dsup gene in human cells was observed to decrease DNA fragmentation induced by X-ray irradiation or treatment with hydrogen peroxide.
evidence: This claim is based on prior published work (Hashimoto et al., 2016).

claim: Dsup-containing human cells exhibited higher viability after X-ray irradiation than control cells.
source: Moreover, Dsup-containing human cells exhibited higher viability after X-ray irradiation than control cells.
evidence: This claim is based on prior published work (Hashimoto et al., 2016).

claim: Dsup was previously shown to interact with free DNA in an apparently nonspecific manner.
source: It was previously shown that Dsup interacts with free DNA in an apparently nonspecific manner (Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Rv Dsup is a largely disordered and highly charged nuclear protein.
source: The R. varieornatus Dsup protein is a largely disordered and highly charged nuclear protein (Figure 1A) (Hashimoto et al., 2016; Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Rv Dsup was purified to greater than 95% homogeneity by affinity chromatography.
source: To study its biochemical properties, we synthesized a FLAG- and His6-tagged version of the full-length protein in Escherichia coli and purified it to greater than 95% homogeneity by affinity chromatography (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the purification data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Rv Dsup binds with a higher affinity to nucleosomes than to free DNA.
source: These experiments revealed that Rv Dsup binds with a higher affinity to nucleosomes than to free DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rv Dsup binds preferentially to mononucleosomes relative to free DNA in a manner that appears to be independent of the specific DNA sequence.
source: Thus, Rv Dsup binds preferentially to mononucleosomes relative to free DNA in a manner that appears to be independent of the specific DNA sequence.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data comparing binding to 5S rDNA and 601 sequences shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: The presence of linker DNA did not substantially alter the efficiency of Rv Dsup binding to nucleosomes.
source: These experiments showed that the presence of linker DNA did not substantially alter the efficiency of Rv Dsup binding to nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C comparing 147 bp and 181 bp DNA-containing nucleosomes.

claim: Rv Dsup binds primarily to the nucleosome core rather than to the linker DNA.
source: It thus appears that Rv Dsup binds primarily to the nucleosome core rather than to the linker DNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that linker DNA does not affect binding efficiency.

claim: The gel shift pattern with Rv Dsup and mononucleosomes is suggestive of the binding of two molecules of Rv Dsup to the nucleosome.
source: This pattern can be seen particularly clearly in the titration of Rv Dsup with 147 bp 5S rDNA mononucleosomes in Figure 2C, and is suggestive of the binding of two molecules of Rv Dsup to the nucleosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gel shift pattern observed in Figure 2C.

claim: The presence of Rv Dsup does not inhibit the efficiency of ACF-mediated chromatin assembly.
source: The presence of Rv Dsup does not inhibit the efficiency of ACF-mediated chromatin assembly, as measured by the DNA supercoiling assay (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The assembly of chromatin with Rv Dsup results in a small but distinct increase in the nucleosome repeat length.
source: Partial MNase digestion analysis showed that the assembly of chromatin with Rv Dsup results in a small but distinct increase in the nucleosome repeat length (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Rv Dsup-bound mononucleosome particles are released from chromatin upon extensive MNase digestion.
source: This experiment revealed that Rv Dsup-bound mononucleosome particles are released from the chromatin upon extensive MNase digestion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The interaction of Rv Dsup with nucleosomes in periodic arrays is similar to the binding of Rv Dsup to mononucleosome particles.
source: It therefore appears that the interaction of Rv Dsup with nucleosomes in periodic arrays, as in Figure 3, is similar to the binding of Rv Dsup to mononucleosome particles, as in Figure 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar gel migration patterns observed in Figures 2 and 3D.

claim: Histone H1 is a major nucleosome-binding protein in animals.
source: Histone H1 is a major nucleosome-binding protein in animals, and it has been found to be present at approximately one molecule per nucleosome (Bates and Thomas, 1981) (reviewed in Woodcock et al., 2006; Happel and Doenecke, 2009; Kalashnikova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Histone H1 has been found to be present at approximately one molecule per nucleosome.
source: Histone H1 is a major nucleosome-binding protein in animals, and it has been found to be present at approximately one molecule per nucleosome (Bates and Thomas, 1981) (reviewed in Woodcock et al., 2006; Happel and Doenecke, 2009; Kalashnikova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Histone H1 and Rv Dsup can bind simultaneously to mononucleosomes.
source: These results indicate that histone H1 and Rv Dsup can bind simultaneously to mononucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The addition of both H1 and Rv Dsup did not alter the efficiency of chromatin assembly.
source: These experiments revealed that the addition of both H1 and Rv Dsup did not alter the efficiency of chromatin assembly, as measured by the DNA supercoiling assay (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The presence of histone H1 and Rv Dsup did not disrupt the periodicity of the nucleosome arrays.
source: Furthermore, the presence of histone H1 and Rv Dsup did not disrupt the periodicity of the nucleosome arrays, as assessed with the partial MNase digestion assay (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Histone H1 and Rv Dsup can bind simultaneously to nucleosomes without substantially altering or disrupting chromatin structure.
source: Thus, histone H1 and Rv Dsup can bind simultaneously to nucleosomes, and this binding does not substantially alter or disrupt chromatin structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: The findings that H1 and Dsup can bind simultaneously without disrupting chromatin are consistent with the observation that Rv Dsup is not deleterious to histone H1-containing human cells.
source: These findings are consistent with the observation that Rv Dsup is not deleterious to histone H1-containing human cells (Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior observations cited from Hashimoto et al., 2016.

claim: R. varieornatus and H. exemplaris are limnoterrestrial tardigrades in the family Hypsibiidae.
source: R. varieornatus and H. exemplaris are limnoterrestrial tardigrades in the family Hypsibiidae, and both animals can undergo anhydrobiosis (see, for example, Horikawa et al., 2008; Kondo et al., 2015; Wright, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both R. varieornatus and H. exemplaris can undergo anhydrobiosis.
source: R. varieornatus and H. exemplaris are limnoterrestrial tardigrades in the family Hypsibiidae, and both animals can undergo anhydrobiosis (see, for example, Horikawa et al., 2008; Kondo et al., 2015; Wright, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dsup was initially not identified in H. exemplaris.
source: Dsup was initially not identified in H. exemplaris (Yoshida et al., 2017), but further analysis revealed a Dsup-like protein in this organism (Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Further analysis revealed a Dsup-like protein in H. exemplaris.
source: Dsup was initially not identified in H. exemplaris (Yoshida et al., 2017), but further analysis revealed a Dsup-like protein in this organism (Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The H. exemplaris Dsup-like protein has 26.4% amino acid identity with Rv Dsup.
source: The H. exemplaris Dsup-like protein was found to have 26.4% amino acid identity with Rv Dsup as well as hydrophobicity and charge profiles that are similar to those of Rv Dsup.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis cited from Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017.

claim: The H. exemplaris Dsup-like protein has hydrophobicity and charge profiles that are similar to those of Rv Dsup.
source: The H. exemplaris Dsup-like protein was found to have 26.4% amino acid identity with Rv Dsup as well as hydrophobicity and charge profiles that are similar to those of Rv Dsup.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis cited from Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017.

claim: The Dsup-related genes in both R. varieornatus and H. exemplaris are flanked by the same neighboring genes.
source: This analysis revealed that the Dsup-related genes in both organisms are flanked by the same neighboring genes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The H. exemplaris Dsup-like protein and R. varieornatus Dsup are homologs.
source: Hence, based on the similarity of the proteins, including the closely related nuclear localization signals near the C-termini (Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017), and the similarity of the gene arrangements (Figure 5A), it appeared likely that the H. exemplaris Dsup-like protein and R. varieornatus Dsup are homologs.
evidence: This is an inference based on protein similarity, gene arrangement, and citation to prior work.

claim: He Dsup binds preferentially to nucleosomes relative to free DNA.
source: We then tested the binding of He Dsup to mononucleosomes and to free DNA, and found that He Dsup binds preferentially to nucleosomes relative to free DNA (Figure 5C), as does Rv Dsup (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: He Dsup and Rv Dsup each shift mononucleosomes to approximately the same position on the gel.
source: In addition, we directly compared the binding of He Dsup and Rv Dsup to mononucleosomes, and observed that each of the proteins shifts mononucleosomes to approximately the same position on the gel (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The slower migration of the Rv Dsup-nucleosome complexes relative to that of the He Dsup-nucleosome complexes is consistent with the larger size of Rv Dsup compared to He Dsup.
source: The slower migration of the Rv Dsup-nucleosome complexes relative to that of the He Dsup-nucleosome complexes is consistent with the larger size of Rv Dsup (445 amino acid residues) compared to He Dsup (328 amino acid residues).
evidence: This is an inference based on the gel migration data and protein sizes.

claim: The H. exemplaris Dsup-like protein and R. varieornatus Dsup are orthologs.
source: Therefore, in the analysis of Rv Dsup and He Dsup, the relationship between the proteins (Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017), the similarity of the gene arrangements (Figure 5A), and the conserved biochemical function (Figures 2, 5C and D) lead to the conclusion that the two proteins are orthologs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence including sequence similarity, gene arrangement, and functional conservation.

claim: Ionizing radiation and hydrogen peroxide both generate hydroxyl radicals as a major reactive oxygen species in cells.
source: Because ionizing radiation and hydrogen peroxide both generate hydroxyl radicals as a major reactive oxygen species in cells (Halliwell and Gutteridge, 1992; Stadtman, 1993; Riley, 1994), we investigated whether purified Dsup affects hydroxyl radical-mediated DNA cleavage in a purified and defined biochemical system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the absence of Dsup, the 3.3 kb plasmid DNA was mostly degraded to DNA fragments ranging from 100 to 1000 nt by hydroxyl radicals.
source: In the absence of Dsup, the 3.3 kb plasmid DNA was mostly degraded to DNA fragments ranging from 100 to 1000 nt (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The extent of cleavage of free plasmid DNA by hydroxyl radicals was nearly the same as the amount of cleavage of chromatin.
source: Notably, the extent of cleavage of free plasmid DNA was nearly the same as the amount of cleavage of chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The presence of approximately one nucleosome per 200 bp DNA only slightly protects the DNA from hydroxyl radicals.
source: Thus, the presence of approximately one nucleosome per 200 bp DNA only slightly protects the DNA from hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that free DNA and chromatin are cleaved to similar extents.

claim: Hydroxyl radicals can cleave DNA in nucleosomes.
source: These results are consistent with the previous observation that hydroxyl radicals can cleave DNA in nucleosomes (Hayes et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Upon addition of Rv Dsup, substantial protection of free DNA as well as chromatin from hydroxyl radicals was observed.
source: Upon addition of Rv Dsup, we observed substantial protection of free DNA as well as chromatin from hydroxyl radicals (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Dsup-mediated protection was stronger with chromatin than with free DNA.
source: The Dsup-mediated protection was stronger with chromatin than with free DNA, possibly because the specific binding of Dsup to nucleosomes creates a highly resistant structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and includes a speculative explanation.

claim: In the presence of 4 molecules of Rv Dsup per 200 bp DNA in chromatin, there was a considerable amount of full-length linear DNA remaining after hydroxyl radical-mediated cleavage.
source: In the presence of 4 molecules of Rv Dsup per 200 bp DNA (approximately 4 Dsup molecules per nucleosome) in chromatin, there was a considerable amount of full-length linear DNA remaining after hydroxyl radical-mediated cleavage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rv Dsup is able to protect chromatin from the damaging effects of hydroxyl radicals.
source: These results indicate that Rv Dsup is able to protect chromatin from the damaging effects of hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Hydroxyl radicals react primarily with hydrogen atoms that are exposed in the minor groove of DNA.
source: Because hydroxyl radicals react primarily with hydrogen atoms that are exposed in the minor groove of DNA (Balasubramanian et al., 1998), it appears likely that Dsup blocks access to the minor groove.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Dsup likely blocks access to the minor groove of DNA.
source: Because hydroxyl radicals react primarily with hydrogen atoms that are exposed in the minor groove of DNA (Balasubramanian et al., 1998), it appears likely that Dsup blocks access to the minor groove.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the mechanism of hydroxyl radical action and the protective effect of Dsup.

claim: Rv Dsup provides slightly more protection against hydroxyl radicals than He Dsup.
source: As seen in Figure 6B, we consistently observed that Rv Dsup provides slightly more protection against hydroxyl radicals than He Dsup.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TFIIB did not confer any detectable protection of chromatin from hydroxyl radical-mediated DNA cleavage.
source: In contrast to Dsup, TFIIB did not confer any detectable protection of chromatin from hydroxyl radical-mediated DNA cleavage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Dsup binds to nucleosomes and protects DNA from cleavage by hydroxyl radicals.
source: Thus, these findings collectively indicate that Dsup binds to nucleosomes and protects DNA from cleavage by hydroxyl radicals (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figures 6A and 6B, and illustrated in the model in Figure 6C.

claim: A segment in the C-terminal region of the Dsup proteins exhibits sequence similarity to a conserved sequence in the nucleosome-binding domain of HMGN proteins.
source: This analysis led to the identification of sequence similarity between a segment in the C-terminal region of the Dsup proteins and a conserved sequence in the nucleosome-binding domain of HMGN proteins (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: HMGN proteins are abundant nucleosome-binding proteins that have been found only in vertebrates.
source: The HMGN proteins are abundant nucleosome-binding proteins that have been found only in vertebrates (for reviews, see: Kugler et al., 2012; González-Romero et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: HMGN proteins bind to two high affinity sites on nucleosomes in a manner that is independent of the DNA sequence.
source: They bind to two high affinity sites on nucleosomes in a manner that is independent of the DNA sequence.
evidence: This is a statement about HMGN proteins based on established knowledge.

claim: The nucleosome-binding domain of the HMGN proteins contains a conserved core sequence, RRSARLSA, which is critical for the binding of HMGN proteins to nucleosomes.
source: The nucleosome-binding domain of the HMGN proteins has been identified, and it contains a conserved core sequence, RRSARLSA, which is critical for the binding of HMGN proteins to nucleosomes (Ueda et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Both Dsup proteins contain a sequence that is similar to the RRSARLSA consensus.
source: Strikingly, both Dsup proteins contain a sequence that is similar to the RRSARLSA consensus (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The M1 mutant Dsup is nearly completely defective for binding to nucleosomes.
source: These experiments revealed that the M1 mutant Dsup is nearly completely defective for binding to nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The C-terminal region of Rv Dsup (from amino acid residues 360 to 445) is essential for nucleosome binding.
source: Hence, the C-terminal region of Rv Dsup (from amino acid residues 360 to 445) is essential for nucleosome binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the M1 mutant data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The M2 mutant Dsup exhibits reduced binding to nucleosomes.
source: In addition, the M2 mutant Dsup exhibits reduced binding to nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The HMGN-like sequence in Dsup is important for its binding to nucleosomes.
source: Thus, the HMGN-like sequence in Dsup is important for its binding to nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the M2 mutant data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The nucleosome-binding-deficient M1 mutant Dsup is nearly completely defective for protection of chromatin against hydroxyl radicals.
source: These experiments revealed that the nucleosome-binding-deficient M1 mutant Dsup is nearly completely defective for protection of chromatin against hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The M2 mutant Dsup is partially defective for protection against hydroxyl radicals.
source: We also observed that the M2 mutant Dsup is partially defective for protection against hydroxyl radicals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The binding of Dsup to nucleosomes is required to protect chromatin from hydroxyl radical-mediated DNA damage.
source: These data support the model that the binding of Dsup to nucleosomes is required to protect chromatin from hydroxyl radical-mediated DNA damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutant data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Dsup is a tardigrade-specific factor.
source: Here we have found that Dsup, a tardigrade-specific factor, is a nucleosome-binding protein that protects chromosomal DNA from hydroxyl radical-mediated cleavage.
evidence: This is a statement based on the current understanding that Dsup has only been found in tardigrades.

claim: The findings provide a molecular explanation for the ability of Dsup to protect DNA in human cells from degradation by ionizing radiation or by treatment with hydrogen peroxide.
source: These findings provide a molecular explanation for the ability of Dsup to protect DNA in human cells from degradation by ionizing radiation or by treatment with hydrogen peroxide (Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior observations.

claim: Dsup protects the tardigrade genome from hydroxyl radical-mediated damage under diverse conditions.
source: More generally, these results suggest that Dsup protects the tardigrade genome from hydroxyl radical-mediated damage under diverse conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Protection of the tardigrade genome from hydroxyl radicals may contribute to survival after extended periods in the anhydrobiotic state.
source: For instance, protection of the tardigrade genome from hydroxyl radicals may contribute to survival after extended periods in the anhydrobiotic state (Wełnicz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement with citation to relevant literature.

claim: Both R. varieornatus and H. exemplaris appear to contain histone H1.
source: Both R. varieornatus and H. exemplaris appear to contain histone H1, and it is thus likely that Dsup normally acts in conjunction with H1.
evidence: This is an inference based on general knowledge about eukaryotic chromatin.

claim: Dsup likely normally acts in conjunction with histone H1.
source: Both R. varieornatus and H. exemplaris appear to contain histone H1, and it is thus likely that Dsup normally acts in conjunction with H1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Dsup and H1 can bind simultaneously to nucleosomes.

claim: Dsup functions in histone H1-containing human cells.
source: In this regard, it is also notable that Dsup functions in histone H1-containing human cells (Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on prior published work.

claim: Rv Dsup and He Dsup are orthologs.
source: Rv Dsup and He Dsup are orthologs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the paper.

claim: The identification of Dsup as a chromatin-protective protein in two species suggests that it is a key factor that contributes to the unique properties of tardigrades.
source: Instead, the identification of Dsup as a chromatin-protective protein in two species suggests that it is a key factor that contributes to the unique properties of tardigrades.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings in two tardigrade species.

claim: HMGN proteins have been found only in vertebrates.
source: Because the HMGN proteins have been found only in vertebrates (González-Romero et al., 2015), the origin of the HMGN-like sequences in the tardigrade Dsup proteins is, at present, a mystery.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The origin of the HMGN-like sequences in the tardigrade Dsup proteins is, at present, a mystery.
source: Because the HMGN proteins have been found only in vertebrates (González-Romero et al., 2015), the origin of the HMGN-like sequences in the tardigrade Dsup proteins is, at present, a mystery.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the unexplained evolutionary relationship.

claim: It is possible but not likely that the Dsup and HMGN proteins provide a very rare example of sequence convergence.
source: It is possible but not likely (see, for example, Doolittle, 1994) that the Dsup and HMGN proteins provide a very rare example of sequence convergence.
evidence: This is a speculative statement with citation to relevant literature.

claim: The Dsup proteins are highly charged and largely disordered.
source: The Dsup proteins are highly charged and largely disordered (Hashimoto et al., 2016; Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Dsup proteins are enriched in serine, alanine, glycine, and lysine (SAGK) residues.
source: With respect to the latter, examination of the amino acid composition of the Dsup proteins reveals that they are enriched in serine, alanine, glycine, and lysine (SAGK) residues.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the amino acid composition of Dsup proteins.

claim: Rv Dsup contains more than 60% SAGK residues.
source: Rv Dsup contains more than 60% SAGK residues, and He Dsup has over 50% SAGK residues.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the amino acid composition of Rv Dsup.

claim: He Dsup has over 50% SAGK residues.
source: Rv Dsup contains more than 60% SAGK residues, and He Dsup has over 50% SAGK residues.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the amino acid composition of He Dsup.

claim: SAGK are disorder-promoting amino acids.
source: SAGK are disorder-promoting amino acids (Dunker et al., 2001), and the SAGK residues may form a diffuse mass of protein that protects the chromosomal DNA from hydroxyl radical-mediated cleavage in a variety of conditions (Figure 6C).
